item.title: [RIEG] Masculinidades en transformación: Debates y tensiones de género en México
item.dc:creator: Nelson Florez Vaquiro
item.description:
Nelson Florez Vaquiro

Revista Interdisciplinaria de Estudios de Género de El Colegio de México, vol. 12, pp. 1-8 · publicado 2026-11-09

Hombres y relaciones de género en México, de Olga Lorena Rojas, ofrece una revisión amplia de la investigación social sobre las masculinidades y las relaciones de género en el país. Esta reseña examina los cinco ejes que estructuran la obra: el marco conceptual sobre masculinidades y trayectorias de vida, la sexualidad, la proveeduría económica, el trabajo doméstico y de cuidados, y la relación entre el trabajo remunerado de las mujeres y la violencia masculina en el hogar. Se destaca como principal aporte del libro la demostración de que las masculinidades no constituyen identidades homogéneas, sino configuraciones atravesadas por desigualdades de clase, territorio y generación, y de que las transformaciones de género en México son asimétricas y no lineales. Asimismo, se analiza cómo los cambios demográficos, laborales y familiares de las últimas décadas tensionan los mandatos tradicionales de proveeduría y autoridad masculina, que se reconfiguran sin desaparecer y coexisten con desigualdades estructurales persistentes.

item.title: [The Americas] Conjuring Columbia: Phillis Wheatley’s Goddess, Miranda’s Colombia, and Hemispheric Limits on Imagining Armed People of Color, 1775–1807
item.dc:creator: Lina Del Castillo
item.description:
Lina Del Castillo

The Americas: A Quarterly Review of Latin American History, pp. 1-33 · publicado 2026-11-09

Why is “Colombia,” in South America, not spelled “Columbia”? And what can the largely forgotten history behind this orthographic divergence reveal? Two remarkable figures from the Age of Revolutions, Phillis Wheatley and Francisco de Miranda, are rarely considered together to answer these questions. After publishing her first book of poetry in 1773, Wheatley gained freedom from slavery and dedicated a poem to General George Washington, who had it published in 1776. Her poem was the first to fully personify through mythic allegory the golden-haired goddess “Columbia,” who subtly called in armies (inclusive of people of color) to win freedom from Britannia. Wheatley’s poetic moves galvanized a US audience. By 1784, when Miranda claimed to have met Wheatley in Boston, Columbia was everywhere, yet few attributed the goddess to Wheatley’s poetic prowess, and most ignored Wheatley’s careful deployment of Columbia’s inclusive army. Realizing “Columbia’s” value as shorthand for New World independence, Miranda plucked “Columbia” from the North American context and adjusted her name to Spanish-language spelling conventions. Miranda’s linguistic move, given “Columbia’s” already existing popularity, helped him gain transatlantic notoriety for “Colombian” independence from Spain. Delving into eighteenth–nineteenth-century poetry, correspondence, and print culture demonstrates how Wheatley’s “Columbia” inspired Miranda’s “Colombia,” and, in turn, how this poetic geopolitical vision helped make thinkable transatlantic imaginaries of freedom. For both Wheatley and Miranda, their Columbian/Colombian imaginaries included people of color among the ranks of her liberating armies, yet their calls for inclusion required careful calibration (and at times erasure).

item.title: [Gender & History] New Goods and New Habits: Cleanliness as a Class Marker and the Making of the Peasant Homemaker, Sweden 1850–1910
item.dc:creator: Marie Ulväng
item.description:
Marie Ulväng

Gender & History · publicado 2026-11-06

The article examines what cleanliness, that is, hygiene and tidiness, meant for landowning farm households in the county of Härjedalen in the inland of northern Sweden from the 1860s to the 1910s. The period is characterised by a growing understanding of bacteria and of how infectious diseases could be prevented through improved hygiene, leading towards a ‘germ panic’. In Härjedalen, the industrialisation of forestry led many farm households to sell their homesteads, leaving landowning farm households a small but influential group in local society. The study shows that wealthier farm households improved their houses and adopted bourgeois customs and attitudes to cleanliness to distinguish themselves from the landless peasantry. The shift in the main source of income from livestock farming to forestry altered the dynamics of men's and women's tasks and responsibilities, enabling wives to devote more time to housework. The increase in domestic work and the reallocation of labour were not driven by fear of bacteria or by social pressure from above, but by cleanliness and housewifery as markers of social class. Spacious and well‐kept homes were not an option for the areas’ workers, crofters and tenants.

item.title: [Gender & History] “What Roles for Women?”: Gendering the New International Economic Order at the UN Regional Economic Commission for Africa
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Banks
item.description:
Elizabeth Banks

Gender & History · publicado 2026-11-06

The 1974 declaration of the New International Economic Order (NIEO), which came just ahead of the UN's International Women's Year (IWY) in 1975, attempted a major renegotiation of global inequality without reference to gender. Through the rest of the 1970s, women at the African Training and Research Centre for Women (ATRCW) in Addis Ababa, itself an initiative of the IWY, leveraged the power of the NIEO to support their undervalued work on African women's economic lives. Exploring their work sheds light on the geography of gendered intellectual labor of development work in international organizations during the age of decolonization and foregrounds the importance of small, apparently peripheral sites. Women at ATRCW advocated for women‐centered research designs and for development projects focused on women's work that would harness women as a resource for national development in ways that lasted beyond the NIEO. In doing so, they renegotiated the NIEO based on local evidence and gendered experiences but ultimately accepted its terms.

item.title: [Social Compass] Bat sacrifice as a significant element in Maya earth rituals
item.dc:creator: James E. Brady
item.description:
James E. Brady

Social Compass · publicado 2026-11-05

Maya religion has a heavily terrestrial focus, growing out of the Amerindian belief in Earth as an all-powerful, sacred, and animate entity. Features that penetrate Earth, particularly caves, are revered as sacred landmarks because many of their most important deities are believed to reside in caves. Levy-Bruhl noted that sacred landmarks are not single features but complexes that include the animal species that inhabit those places. Thus, bats were important actors in the Maya’s interaction with their deities. Bat remains appear in several specific ritual contexts. In this article, the author presents evidence to suggest that bats may have accompanied the dead in burials. More importantly, a reanalysis of cave data suggests that the sacrifice of bats may have been a frequent occurrence in caves where bats functioned as messengers to the deities.

item.title: [Social Compass] Why can’t Muslims in Indonesia say ‘Merry Christmas’ in public? Dual integralism and moral sovereignty
item.dc:creator: Justito Adiprasetio
item.description:
Justito Adiprasetio

Social Compass · publicado 2026-11-05

This article examines the recurring controversy over whether Muslims, who form the demographic majority in Indonesia, may say ‘Merry Christmas’, analyzing it as a symptom of dual integralism, the entangled authority of state and Islamic institutions in regulating moral conduct. Through a Foucauldian genealogical lens, the study traces how symbolic disputes are shaped by state integralism, rooted in the homogenizing logic of Pancasila, and Islamic integralism, which seeks to assert religious norms in public life. By analyzing key moments from the 1945 Jakarta Charter debates to the Majelis Ulama Indonesia (Indonesia Ulama Council) fatwas issued in 1981 and 2024, the article shows that moral authority in Indonesia is both contested and co-produced across state and religious institutions. The greeting controversy operates as a proxy for broader struggles over legitimacy and normative control. Within this dual structure, everyday symbolic acts become flashpoints through which Indonesia’s moral and civic boundaries are repeatedly negotiated.

item.title: [LARR] La vida material del silencio: Sobre Verónica Gerber Bicecci, fracturas, cortes y pausas
item.dc:creator: Isabella Vergara C.
item.description:
Isabella Vergara C.

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-24 · publicado 2026-11-06

Este artículo propone una lectura de tres obras de Verónica Gerber Bicecci a partir de la dimensión visual y sonora del silencio, en diálogo con los estudios contemporáneos sobre el sonido, en particular los aportes de Ana María Ochoa Gautier, David Toop y Jean-Luc Nancy, y con una redefinición crítica del collage basada en el trabajo reciente de Freya Gowrley, Fragmentary Forms (2024). Más que un medio o un género, el collage se concibe aquí como una práctica de pensamiento material que desarma la genealogía canónica del papier collé cubista y se plantea como una forma de ensamblaje transhistórica y transmedial. La propuesta central del artículo es pensar el silencio como una materia activa, una zona intersticial que remite a una apertura perceptiva donde las citas, los cortes y los residuos retoman agencia. A partir de un recorrido por una serie visual del silencio en la obra de Gerber Bicecci, el texto analiza dos momentos en los que el silencio se despatriarcaliza al habitar otras materias: Mujeres polilla (2018) y otro día… (poemas sintéticos) (2023). En ambas, el uso de la acetona, el polvo y el residuo activa una poética del emborronamiento que subvierte las oposiciones entre forma y contenido, entre lo decible y lo indecible. El artículo concluye con un análisis de Centón pétreo (2021), donde el collage de citas visuales y literarias fragmentadas dramatiza un silencio que reverbera. En todos los casos, el collage permite visibilizar un tipo de silencio que desborda su definición convencional y opera como una fractura de la forma: un corte material y discursivo que interpela los regímenes de género, las políticas de archivo y las formas de escucha. Así, el silencio deviene en acto indisciplinado que, desde su mínima y fragmentaria materialidad, ensaya otras formas de imaginación política.

item.title: [LARR] Gender and Violence Between the Home and the Street: The Narrative Construction of the Public/Private Boundary in Brazil
item.dc:creator: Natália Otto, Roberta S. Pamplona, Luisa Farah Schwartzman
item.description:
Natália Otto, Roberta S. Pamplona, Luisa Farah Schwartzman

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-18 · publicado 2026-11-06

Latin American scholars have problematized the binary between private gender-based violence and public urban violence, highlighting the interconnection of state, urban, and gendered violence. Yet cultural notions of the public and private continue to inform the “gendering” of violence. In this article, we examine how police officers who investigate murders of women (thirty-six inquiries and nine interviews) and girls incarcerated in a juvenile detention center (twenty-two interviews) in Brazil narrate violence through a differential gendering of the categories of the “home” and the “street.” We find that the street is framed as a space of genderless, (drug) market-related, and expected instrumental violence, and the home is a space of gendered and unexpected emotional violence. This framing reduces gender violence to emotional disputes within the family and naturalizes violence in the “street,” portraying it as unavoidable, thus obscuring and legitimating structural state and gender violence against women.

item.title: [LARR] Words and Wisdom of the Sea: The Indigenous Lexicon of the La Libertad Coast (Peru) in a Historical Perspective
item.dc:creator: Luis Andrade Ciudad, Rafael Vega-Centeno, Denis Torres Menchola, Diego Luza Fernández
item.description:
Luis Andrade Ciudad, Rafael Vega-Centeno, Denis Torres Menchola, Diego Luza Fernández

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-19 · publicado 2026-11-06

A detailed examination of words that can be attributed to Quingnam, the ancient language of Chimor, in Peru’s North Coast, reveals a marked preponderance of sea-related terms. The words of possible Quingnam origin that we have identified refer to activities such as fishing and totora cultivation and make meticulous distinctions between animal and plant species populating the coast. Along with the physical proximity of the Pacific Ocean and its natural resources, this emphasis may also have historical causes, rooted in the role of traditional fishing communities in the structure of colonial domination and their degree of agency therein. Our study combines an assessment of linguistic sources with the application of ethnographically oriented lexical surveys, and dialogues with the scant data on northern Peruvian fishing communities provided by colonial sources.

item.title: [Mexican Studies] Enamorada as Mise-en-Scène of the Myth of the Revolution
item.dc:creator: Matt Losada
item.description:
Matt Losada

Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos, vol. 42, núm. 3, pp. 555-574 · publicado 2026

This article examines how the film Enamorada (Emilio Fernández, 1946) legitimizes the shifting priorities of the Mexican state from the more radical presidency of Lázaro Cárdenas, which fulfilled certain promises of the revolution, toward the more conservative presidencies that followed. Enamorada recasts the revolutionary myth through a romantic union between antagonistic social classes, thus integrating the conservative sectors of the wealthy and the Church into the “revolutionary family.” When the revolutionary general abandons the town of Cholula, he cedes control to the lettered bourgeoisie, the revolutionary ethos cedes to governmentality, and constitutive violence is delegitimized in favor of a constituted violence monopolized by the state.

item.title: [Mexican Studies] “At Last, Abandoned, I Went Out Alone”: Translating Conservatism Among the México de afuera Community (1915–1920)
item.dc:creator: Kevin Anzzolin
item.description:
Kevin Anzzolin

Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos, vol. 42, núm. 3, pp. 523-554 · publicado 2026

This article examines how the community of exiles commonly referred to as México de afuera used literary translation not only as a cultural exercise but as a political strategy. Drawing on translation theorists such as André Lefevere and Itamar Even-Zohar, this work challenges the narrative that conservative exiles isolated themselves in terms of literature and culture. Thus, an examination of the journalistic production of the period (particularly in San Antonio’s La Prensa and Revista Mexicana) allows us to deepen and nuance the arguments presented by Kari Soriano Salkjelsvik among others, who argue that Latin American conservatives, far from remaining on the margins of modernization processes and the accelerated expansion of journalistic media, utilized both technological innovations and the growth of the reading public to disseminate their ideas.

item.title: [Mexican Studies] Impossible to Tame: Insects in Travel Literature on Nineteenth-Century Yucatán and Guatemala
item.dc:creator: María Fernanda Valencia-Suárez, Carolina Depetris, Leila Gabriela Gómez
item.description:
María Fernanda Valencia-Suárez, Carolina Depetris, Leila Gabriela Gómez

Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos, vol. 42, núm. 3, pp. 475-501 · publicado 2026

This article examines insects’ agency in travel writing. Traditionally, scholarship centered on a critique of the traveler’s imperial gaze, and the production of images, maps, and books, among other visual technologies. Our approach focuses on the agency of the insects’ resistance to that “imperial gaze” through their own sensorial world, not always governed by the visual sense. After offering a panoramic view of Western travelers’ encounters with bugs and critters in Yucatan, Central America, and the Caribbean, we closely examine Anne and Alfred Maudslay’s A Glimpse at Guatemala (1899), and Alice Dixon Le Plongeon’s Yucatán: Its Ancient Palaces and Modern Cities (unpublished).

item.title: [Mexican Studies] México en clave japonesa: Helen Hyde y la construcción transcultural de lo mexicano (1911-1914)
item.dc:creator: David Bernal Montero
item.description:
David Bernal Montero

Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos, vol. 42, núm. 3, pp. 502-522 · publicado 2026

Entre 1911 y 1914, la artista estadounidense Helen Hyde (1868-1919) produjo en México grabados que constituyen un ejercicio singular de construcción transnacional del imaginario mexicano. Formada en técnicas del ukiyo-e japonés, Hyde aplicó esta sensibilidad a escenas cotidianas en plena Revolución, generando una representación doblemente mediada y filtrada por los códigos visuales del japonismo y por su posición como mujer artista extranjera. El análisis de cuatro grabados demuestra que el japonismo opera no solo como influencia estética sino como mecanismo de mediación cultural que produce una mexicanidad suavizada, atemporal y consumible que omite el conflicto revolucionario.

item.title: [Mexican Studies] Medio ambiente y paisaje potosino a inicios del siglo XIX: la estadística de 1825
item.dc:creator: Alejandro Morón-Ríos, Sergio Alejandro Cañedo Gamboa
item.description:
Alejandro Morón-Ríos, Sergio Alejandro Cañedo Gamboa

Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos, vol. 42, núm. 3, pp. 442-474 · publicado 2026

Este artículo presenta una reconstrucción del paisaje entre 1825 y 1826 en cinco municipios del estado de San Luis Potosí, México, ubicados en condiciones ambientales distintas. La minería, actividad principal en Real de Catorce, propició una alta densidad poblacional y requirió de gran cantidad de ganado, provocando la pérdida de sus bosques al final del siglo XVIII. El área de Rioverde tenía haciendas de gran tamaño con vocación agrícola y ganadera que definieron su paisaje y generaron una menor alteración del medio ambiente. Por su parte, en la región de la Huasteca, el paisaje fue moldeado por los cultivos básicos, una ganadería menor y una explotación forestal incipiente, factores que generaron cambios menores en el medio ambiente.

item.title: [Gender & History] Negotiating Intimate Boundaries: Gender, Sexuality, and Migration in 1960s West Germany
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth Kimmerle
item.description:
Elisabeth Kimmerle

Gender & History · publicado 2026-11-05

In the 1960s, the children of unmarried women migrant workers in West Germany became a transnational political case that occupied federal and state authorities, social workers, and consulates. Reproductive matters embodied a state of vulnerability for migrant women who not only feared stigmatization in their home countries, but also faced deportation if they did not give up their children for adoption and had to receive welfare benefits. This article explores the ways in which gender and sexuality deeply shaped labor migration and, as a result, politicized migrants’ private and intimate relations. It argues that pregnancy among unmarried migrant women became a site of conflicting interests of the West German and Turkish migration regimes. Within the constrained space between those two migration regimes, migrant women developed precarious forms of agency such as transnational adoption and abortion. Drawing on archival sources, oral history interviews, and Turkish newspaper reports, the article aims to contribute to the historiography of migration from a gender‐historical perspective that allows for a nuanced understanding of the complex ways in which intimate modes became political points of contention.

item.title: [LARR] Un museo de pieles humanas: La colección de tatuajes de José María Garavito Baraya. Colombia, 1890–1970
item.dc:creator: Miguel Adolfo Galindo Pérez
item.description:
Miguel Adolfo Galindo Pérez

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-21 · publicado 2026-11-05

Este artículo explora la historia del tatuaje en Colombia en la primera mitad del siglo XX, evaluando sus usos como dispositivo de conocimiento anatómico en la medicina legal y sus principales características identitarias, prácticas materiales e iconográficas. A través del análisis de una colección de tatuajes disecados reunidos por José María Garavito Baraya, se exploran las estrategias intelectuales y operaciones concretas con las que, desde la medicina, se coleccionó, representó y fetichizó el cuerpo tatuado. A partir de ello, se analizarán los insumos visuales, técnicas de elaboración y sus contextos de producción tanto como marca corporal e insumo forense. La materialidad de estos artefactos revela al tatuaje como un objeto de escrutinio científico sobre el cual se establecieron estigmas y taxonomías asociadas al crimen y la enfermedad, basadas en expresiones visuales, surgidas dentro de una sociedad que lo evocó positivamente como una expresión de relaciones personales, sociales y religiosas.

item.title: [Debate Feminista] Pintar para salvar la vida. Sally Gabori, memoria y reparación
item.dc:creator: María Teresa Martín Palomo
item.description:
María Teresa Martín Palomo

Debate Feminista, vol. 73, pp. 1-23 · publicado 2026-11-02

La obra de Sally Gabori, singular artista de la comunidad Kaiardilt, en Australia, es un acto de cuidado y reparación frente al borrado colonial. Empieza a pintar con 81 años, y sus lienzos dan cuenta de su lengua, su cultura, su pueblo y el territorio en que vivió su infancia hasta que un desastre natural, en forma de ciclón y maremoto, obliga a su comunidad a trasladarse a otra isla en la que se impone una política de segregación por la que niños y niñas son separados de sus progenitores, de su lengua materna y sus referentes culturales. Convierte así al arte en un espacio de resistencia y de justicia poética; también en un espacio de cuidados y de construcción colectiva, en tanto que muchos de sus lienzos monumentales son realizados con sus hijas y otras mujeres de su pueblo. Pintar con cuidado no es solo una forma de expresión, es una forma creativa de mantener vivo su pueblo, su legado y su cultura, aun cuando su lengua esté a punto de perderse ya para siempre.

item.title: [LARR] Breaking the Ice: Contributions and Challenges for Andean Glaciological Research Led by Women
item.dc:creator: Ana Huaico-Malhue, Edilia Jaque, Ana Guadalupe Hernández-Duarte, Marion San Juan Díaz, Mariajosé Herrera-Ossandón, Elizabet Lizama, Beatriz Cid Aguayo
item.description:
Ana Huaico-Malhue, Edilia Jaque, Ana Guadalupe Hernández-Duarte, Marion San Juan Díaz, Mariajosé Herrera-Ossandón, Elizabet Lizama, Beatriz Cid Aguayo

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-22 · publicado 2026-11-02

This study examines the participation of women in Andean glaciology over the past four decades, combining a bibliometric analysis of 204 peer-reviewed articles (1983–2022) and a survey of female first authors (2018–2022). Results show a steady increase in women-led publications, rising from 8 percent in the 1980s–1990s to 30 percent in the past decade. However, structural barriers, including unequal access to funding, resistance to female leadership, and the disproportionate burden of caregiving, continue to limit gender equity in the field. Women-led studies are concentrated in Argentina and Chile, while countries like Colombia, Bolivia, and Venezuela remain underrepresented. The methods most commonly used by female researchers are fieldwork and remote sensing, which reflects limited access to laboratory-based approaches. Survey responses highlight both the motivations (scientific interest, conservation) and challenges (discrimination, lack of recognition, work-life imbalance) faced by women scientists. The findings reveal persistent epistemic and territorial asymmetries, especially in the context of international research led by Global North institutions. The study underscores the need for inclusive policies that go beyond formal representation, supporting equitable research leadership and collaboration. Promoting gender equity in cryosphere science is not only a matter of justice; it is essential for generating contextually relevant, socially just, and scientifically robust responses to climate change in the Andes.

El objetivo de este artículo es realizar un análisis autoetnográfico feminista sobre la relación entre duelo, cuidados y academia. Recupero la ética del cuidado y la antropología feminista para definir al duelo como un trabajo de cuidados que nos permite sostener la vida y la muerte en un mundo en pérdida y doliente. Bajo estas coordenadas teóricas, realizó los siguientes análisis autoetnográficos: 1) el recorrido sobre cómo el duelo aparece como un trabajo de cuidados dirigido a la persona fallecida, así como a múltiples seres vivos y no vivos en el contexto de la pérdida, 2) el análisis sobre el entrecruce entre duelo, cuidados y trabajo académico, y su impacto en las mujeres académicas; 3) el rescate de prácticas de cuidados realizadas por mujeres académicas y no académicas para sostener a otras mujeres académicas.

item.description:

El orden social de género ha configurado el trabajo de cuidados como un mandato social que recae en las mujeres. Este trabajo de cuidados habitualmente es no remunerado, no reconocido y está investido de aspectos morales y afectivos; hay sanciones sociales y familiares cuando no se realiza. Algunas de las mujeres académicas recurren a la no maternidad como estrategia para consolidar su carrera académica o posponen la maternidad (Castañeda y Contreras, 2019; Castañeda, 2016), otras buscan estrategias para conciliar maternidad con academia, no sin desgaste, culpa o cansancio (Contreras, 2019). Sin embargo, esto no exime a las académicas de cuidar, ya que despliegan prácticas de cuidado hacia otros actores. Este trabajo busca comprender y visibilizar el cuidado que las mujeres académicas realizan con padres, hermanos, personas dependientes, o incluso entre pares o estudiantes. Todo ello a partir de entrevistas a mujeres académicas de la Universidad de Guadalajara.

item.title: [Debate Feminista] Condiciones neoliberales de la maternidad: tensiones y afectos en académicas
item.dc:creator: Mariana Lugo Arellano
item.description:
Mariana Lugo Arellano

Debate Feminista, vol. 73, pp. 1-30 · publicado 2026-10-28

Este artículo problematiza el modelo de maternidad de mujeres académicas en el marco de las condiciones neoliberales, a partir del entorno, los ideales regulatorios, las estrategias de cuidado y los afectos del vínculo materno. Mediante una metodología cualitativa con enfoque biográfico, se analiza la experiencia materna de profesoras-investigadoras de tiempo completo en Instituciones de Educación Superior o Centros Públicos de Investigación de la Ciudad de México, que tuvieron su primer hijx a partir de los 30 años en pareja heterosexual. Se identifican rupturas intergeneracionales en los saberes de crianza que se compensan con conocimiento especializado, lo que genera responsabilidad y angustia asociadas a la maternidad intensiva. Sin embargo, se confirma la centralidad de la red de apoyo para el cuidado. En momentos de sobrecarga, la redistribución de responsabilidades revela sus efectos positivos y pone en evidencia la potencia afectiva de la interdependencia en el vínculo materno.

item.title: [Debate Feminista] Trabajo de cuidados y trabajo académico en mujeres adultas mayores
item.dc:creator: Verónica Montes de Oca Zavala, María Concepción Arroyo Rueda
item.description:
Verónica Montes de Oca Zavala, María Concepción Arroyo Rueda

Debate Feminista, vol. 73, pp. 1-32 · publicado 2026-10-28

Las mujeres académicas enfrentan durante su curso de vida sobrecarga de actividades laborales y familiares. Este artículo pretende evidenciar los procesos de cuidados de mujeres académicas al inicio de la trayectoria laboral y reproductiva y al inicio de su etapa de vejez y de cuidados de familiares longevos. La metodología se basó en un cuestionario en línea que registró datos sociodemográficos, experiencias de cuidado familiar y las condiciones laborales en que se insertaron. La evidencia muestra que las mujeres académicas vivieron procesos históricos por cohorte que definieron la secuencia de eventos en su vida laboral y familiar. El cuidado llegó a conflictuar estos ámbitos y generar emociones como culpa, estrés y frustración. Con el paso del tiempo las mujeres académicas se enfrentan a su autocuidado y al cuidado de otras generaciones ascendentes y descendentes.

item.title: [Debate Feminista] Sexual Harassment and its Impact Among Women Students with Disabilities in Ethiopian Universities
item.dc:creator: Tizita Kassahun Gebremariam
item.description:
Tizita Kassahun Gebremariam

Debate Feminista, vol. 73, pp. 1-28 · publicado 2026-10-29

This study explores the intersectional oppressions driving sexual harassment among women students with disabilities in Ethiopian universities, utilizing narrative interviews with twelve participants. The findings revealed a range of sexual harassment, including verbal and nonverbal conduct such as unwanted jokes, physical contact, sex requests for support, and rape attempts. Structural drivers intersect with poverty, disability, gender, and attitudinal problems, causing intersectional vulnerability. The participant women highlight hesitance to report harassment due to stigma, lack of support, peers and staff distrust, and fears of losing assistance. Consequently, they found themselves between survival and safety, which significantly influences their coping strategies. The article argues that the double bind illustrates the need to shift the focus toward institutional responsibilities and commitments in addressing intersectional marginalization and fostering inclusive environments.

item.dc:creator: María de Lourdes Velasco Domínguez, Lucía Espinoza Nieto, Verónica Montes de Oca Zavala

El objetivo del artículo es responder a cómo se organiza el trabajo de cuidado de hijos/as/es de madres científicas en México y cómo incide esta organización en las trayectorias científicas de las madres. El trabajo empleó una metodología cualitativa basada en entrevistas a profundidad a 16 mujeres científicas y madres. Los resultados muestran que, aun cuando el campo científico y el campo de los cuidados son interdependientes, su estructura y su operación se mantienen en tensión. Esto se refleja en las experiencias de conflicto entre el habitus científico y el habitus de cuidado infantil que adoptan las madres científicas. Ellas establecen arreglos familiares con los recursos que les brindan sus posiciones estructurales, lo que influye en la interrupción o continuidad de sus trayectorias científicas.

item.title: [Catholic Hist Rev] The Impact of Peaceful Relations Between the Zayyānid Dynasty and the Iberian Catholic Monarchies on the Kingdom of Tlemcen and the Emirate of Granada from 1482 to 1510
item.dc:creator: Meshal Alenezi, Sanad Abdelfattah
item.description:
Meshal Alenezi, Sanad Abdelfattah

The Catholic Historical Review, vol. 112, núm. 2, pp. 188-213 · publicado 2026-03

Abstract: Between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries, North Africa was home to three major Muslim polities. Among these was the Kingdom of Tlemcen, governed by the Zayyānid (ʽAbd al-Wādids) dynasty (633– 962 AH/1236–1555 CE), which was strategically located between the Ḥafṣīd (627–982 AH/1229–1574 CE) and Marīnīd (614–869 AH/1217–1465 CE) kingdoms. Several scholars have discussed the nature of relations between these states from the thirteenth to the fifteenth century. This paper proposes that the relations among these states led the Kingdom of Tlemcen to foster peaceful relations with the Crowns of Castile and Aragon in the Iberian Peninsula. It also analyzes the impact of these peaceful relations on the relations between the Kingdom of Tlemcen and the last Islamic state in the Iberian Peninsula, the Emirate of Granada. These relations contributed to making the Kingdom of Tlemcen steadfast in the face of conspiracies and attacks from its neighbors. This paper employs a historical method that draws on several primary sources, including Castilian and Zayyānid sources.

item.title: [Catholic Hist Rev] Christ and the Courts of Rome: The Pericope adulterae in Patristic Judicial Thought
item.dc:creator: Maria E. Doerfler

Abstract: This article examines the interpretations of the pericope adulterae, the biblical story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11), made by Ambrose of Milan and Augustine of Hippo in their correspondence with Roman magistrates. Both authors deploy the pericope to argue for the compatibility of the Christian religion and the Roman criminal justice system, locating themselves, their interlocutors, and the criminals charged before them within the pericope’s narrative. Yet Ambrose and Augustine employ different interpretive strategies, which have implications for their ideas concerning the relationship between Church and Empire and divine and human justice. These tensions in exegesis provide an effective lens through which to examine these authors’ respective visions of the political and judicial functions of Christians within the Roman Empire.

Abstract: The July 1, 2026, episcopal consecrations by the Priestly Society of St. Pius X invite renewed historical attention to a movement often treated either as liturgical protest or as canonical anomaly. This article argues that the Society is better understood through a sustained contest over the authoritative narration of Catholic continuity after the Second Vatican Council. item.title: [Catholic Hist Rev] The Translation and Interpretation of the Lunyu ( The Analects ) by the Spanish Dominican Domingo Fernández de Navarrete in the Seventeenth Century
item.dc:creator: Baobao Zhang
item.description:
Baobao Zhang

The Catholic Historical Review, vol. 112, núm. 2, pp. 214-245 · publicado 2026-03

Abstract: In 1676, the Spanish Dominican Domingo Fernández de Navarrete published Tratados históricos, políticos, éticos, y religiosos de la monarchia de China, which contained an abridged Spanish translation of the Lunyu. Navarrete used the early translated texts of the Jesuits as references and quoted them in his own translation. The version of the Lunyu translated by Navarrete was influenced by both Scholasticism and Cheng-Zhu neo-Confucianism (程朱理學), and his translation further reinforces Confucian rationality as presented in the Jesuits’ Sapientia Sinica. Navarrete was also concerned about the Confucian rituals recorded in the Lunyu, which he regarded as a form of superstition and idolatry. If an atheist is regarded as “one who does not know the lord of heaven,” then, in Navarrete’s view, Confucius was a complete atheist. The study of Navarrete’s translation of the Lunyu is conducive to further deepening our understanding of the Chinese Rites Controversy.

item.title: [LARR] Andean Glaciers in Times of Planetary Crisis
item.dc:creator: Cristián Simonetti, Javiera Barandiarán, Jose Ragas
item.description:
Cristián Simonetti, Javiera Barandiarán, Jose Ragas

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-14 · publicado 2026-10-29

This special dossier examines how understandings of Andean glaciers transform under the planetary crisis, defined by humanity’s impact on geophysical processes at a planetary scale. Once regarded as remnants of deep geological time, glaciers have become emblematic casualties of anthropogenic global warming, their accelerated melting compressing geological history into human timescales and raising urgent ethical and political questions about protection, mitigation, and loss. This interdisciplinary collection, including contributions focused on Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, and the wider region, calls for approaches that move beyond universalizing Anthropocene narratives and toward historically and territorially situated accounts of glacial change, challenging colonial and extractivist frameworks that have long shaped the governance of ice and nature. The introduction argues that dominant scientific and state-centered framings—rooted in objectivity, distant observation, and a physicochemical definition of ice—tend to abstract glaciers into universal, placeless indicators of global change, obscuring the local extractivist and colonial dynamics driving their destruction, particularly through mining of critical minerals for a green energy transition. Against this detached view, the dossier foregrounds situated, relational, and often Indigenous conceptions of glaciers as vital entities embedded in organic, social, and spiritual life.

item.title: [Gender & History] Respected and Ignored: British Women and the Arab Revolt (1936–39) in Mandate Palestine
item.dc:creator: Alex Worsfold
item.description:
Alex Worsfold

Gender & History · publicado 2026-10-28

This article aims to reinsert British women and their perspectives into our understanding of anticolonial resistance in Palestine. Historiography on the Arab Revolt (1936–39) has previously been built from colonial state archives that disproportionally speak with a male voice and, as such, rely on certain gendered assumptions to describe the historical participants and events of the period. This article focuses on the records of three British women who worked as teachers during the mandate period, examining how they experienced and understood the anticolonial resistance and violence that occurred around them. It contextualises them within the wider British archive of the Revolt and draws on other experiences across the British Empire to seek to unravel how gender, race and violence intersected in their perception of the events around them.

item.title: [Gender & History] Nature's Ambiguous Sex: The Body as a Feminist Resource in German Naturism Around 1900
item.dc:creator: Johannes Bosch
item.description:
Johannes Bosch

Gender & History · publicado 2026-10-25

While gender relations around 1900 were generally marked by sharp dichotomies grounded in nature and the body, the case of naturism appears paradoxical. An influential movement in Germany, it promoted a reform of the body according to natural principles. While sharing conventional ideas about gender roles, naturist practices—vegetarianism, naturopathy, and nudism—largely refrained from sexing the body. Although scholarship has noted this phenomenon, it has not provided a systematic explanation. This article argues that the absence of sex differentiation in naturist practices can be explained through a praxeological analysis of competing body concepts. It shows that naturists operated with two bodies: an anatomical and a hygienic one. While anatomy justified gender dichotomy, hygiene privileged a non‐sexed model. The article explains the emergence of feminist activism within the naturist movement and contributes to a more nuanced understanding of gender and body history around 1900.

item.title: [LARR] Confronting Gender-Based Violence: Attacks on Women’s Organizations in Central America
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Menjívar, Pamela Neumann
item.description:
Cecilia Menjívar, Pamela Neumann

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-20 · publicado 2026-10-26

Women’s rights organizations in Central America have been key actors in promoting women’s right to a life free of violence and advocating for reproductive rights and other social and economic protections for women and girls. Yet throughout Central America, these organizations have experienced myriad attacks in recent years. In this article, we examine attacks on women’s rights organizations in four Central American countries: Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Nicaragua. Although there are important distinctions among the regimes of these four countries, across all of them, setbacks for women have occurred in contexts characterized by increased militarization, autocratic governance, the incursion of conservative religious ideologies in government policies, and the spread of dangerous misinformation that discredits women’s organizations’ efforts. Within these regimes, women’s organizations have been subjected to intimidation, physical violence, legal threats, and digital harassment. Our analysis identifies patterns in these attacks, showing similarities and differences across the four countries during various temporal moments. To do so, we draw on twenty-nine interviews with twenty-eight women activists, academics, and human rights defenders in the region as well as a compilation of newspaper articles, social media, and independent reports documenting attacks on women’s rights leaders and organizations in the four countries. Efforts to dismantle the work of women’s organizations and committed feminists in Central America provide a window into the gendered dimensions of authoritarian practices in the region.

item.title: [LARR] New Evidence on the Demographics of the Paraguayan War: Revisiting Competing Estimates with Archival Draft Records
item.dc:creator: Bárbara Boggiano
item.description:
Bárbara Boggiano

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-34 · publicado 2026-10-26

The demographic consequences of the Paraguayan War (1864–1870) remain among the most contested in Latin American history, with estimates of population loss ranging from under 20 percent to nearly 70 percent. This article revisits the debate by introducing newly digitized wartime administrative records from the Sección Nueva Encuadernación of the Archivo Nacional de Asunción, documenting draft-eligible males across forty-five districts in late 1867 and early 1868. Linking these records to prewar census benchmarks through a transparent projection methodology, I find that across the forty-two districts with a usable projected denominator, only 10,628 draft-eligible males aged twelve and older were observed against a projected male population of 100,692—roughly one in nine. The result is robust to alternative growth assumptions. Although male absence may reflect death, service, imprisonment, desertion, or displacement, the severity of late-war male scarcity is difficult to reconcile with low-loss interpretations and aligns closely with high-loss scenarios.

item.title: [LARR] Gay Rights in the Age of Democratic Backsliding: Bolsonaro’s Brazil with Reflections on the United States
item.dc:creator: Omar G. Encarnación
item.description:
Omar G. Encarnación

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-19 · publicado 2026-10-26

Democratic backsliding is widely recognized as a threat to gay rights, but it is far from clear why the impact of this political malaise varies from country to country. This article makes the case for two variables as the key factors shaping the fate of gay rights in backsliding democracies: democratic resilience and the grounding of gay rights. It shows how under the illiberal and homophobic administration of Jair Bolsonaro (2019–2022), gay rights in Brazil not only survived but also thrived. The country’s biggest gay rights victory—the criminalization of homophobia and transphobia—came under Bolsonaro’s watch. The analysis shows that gay rights in Brazil (and in contrast to the United States) were protected by the capacity of political institutions to defend democracy and a robust civic response to democratic threats. Less apparent is the firm grounding of gay rights in Brazil, which this article argues is owed to the framing of gay rights as a human rights matter rather than as a legal issue.

item.title: [LARR] Post-National Tangos: Exile and Cultural Legitimation in El pretexto de París (Jorge Asís, 1985) and Informe de París (Paula Wajsman, 1990)
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo López Martínez
item.description:
Rodrigo López Martínez

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-16 · publicado 2026-10-26

This article examines two novels that drew on the themes and tropes of tango to depict Argentine exile in Paris in the aftermath of the 1976–1983 dictatorship: Jorge Asís’s El pretexto de París (1985) and Paula Wajsman’s Informe de París (1990). These novels fictionalized Paris through the lens of Argentine culture to present controversial standpoints regarding issues that were heatedly debated at the time, such as the figure of the exiled intellectual and human rights activism. Moreover, both Asís and Wajsman designed their main characters and self-representations as authors by reimagining the gender archetypes of tango in the Parisian context. A cultural form particular to the Río de la Plata, tango allowed them to challenge the paradigm of the Latin American author favored in Europe during the 1980s, which was commonly associated with political commitment and the figures of the Boom. On the one hand, Asís reappropriated the opportunism and artfulness of the compadrito through a sexualized use of language that allegorized his masculine conquest of literary prestige. On the other hand, Wajsman reimagined the figure of the milonguita to reaffirm her independence as a woman and subvert gendered and neocolonial forms of cultural recognition.

item.title: [Gender & History] Thinking With Care About Animals in Medicine and Veterinary Medicine: Gender and the Politics of Care in Scotland, 1910–30
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Vander Meer, Alette Willis
item.description:
Elizabeth Vander Meer, Alette Willis

Gender & History · publicado 2026-10-24

In this article, we ‘think with care’ about gender in Scotland in the early twentieth century, undertaking an ethnographic approach to the archive of OneKind, formerly the Scottish Society for the Prevention of Vivisection (SSPV), which has only recently been catalogued. In exploring the development of the SSPV from its beginnings in 1911 to 1930, we draw on Joan Tronto's definition of care and Puig de la Bellacasa's three dimensions of care: labour/work, affect/affections and ethics/politics. We argue that the SSPV, founded and largely run by women, employed gendered discourse rooted in a distinctive gendered politics of care embedded in Scottish evangelical Christian socialism; this gendered politics has not been the focus of previous historical research. This context of Christian socialism in Scotland created a milieu in which the women of the SSPV, positioned by their gender as natural bearers of compassion, led campaigns. They articulated a duty of gendered care towards animals and expanded a conception of brotherhood (fraternity) that demanded social change. By focusing on specific relationalities and explanations surrounding meanings of care in Scotland, we deepen our awareness of where we are today and how we got here. Understanding the gendered history of care between humans and other animals is essential to finding effective ways to move forward in caring about and for the nonhuman.

item.title: [Gender & History] Milk and Bondage: Enslaved Wet Nurses in the Eighteenth‐Century Cape Colony
item.dc:creator: Eva Marie Lehner
item.description:
Eva Marie Lehner

Gender & History · publicado 2026-10-23

This article examines the social history of enslaved wet nurses in the eighteenth‐century Cape Colony, arguing that the romanticised depiction of these women within settler households was not a softening of the system of slavery but an integral part of how it functioned. Drawing on criminal records from the Court of Justice, petitions to the Council of Police and church council records and read against the grain of their colonial production, the article centres on three case studies: Jacomijn, whose lactating body was hired out while her own infant was left without care, resulting in the child's death; Sara, whose wet‐nursing labour was entangled with sexual exploitation by a European settler and whose child remained legally the property of her enslaver; and Hanna and Catryn, a mother and daughter rented out across two generations by the Dutch East India Company, whose manumission was secured through an exchange of enslaved men. Using the analytical framework of dependency, the article demonstrates how the affective language of colonial documents (from Lady Anne Barnard's sketch of an ‘imperfect sleeping Madonna’ to the Dutch term minnemoer, meaning ‘love mother’) operated in concert with, rather than in tension with, the transactional logic of reproductive labour extraction.

item.title: [The Americas] The Taller de Escritores of the University of Concepción and the Cold War
item.dc:creator: Patrick Iber
item.description:
Patrick Iber

The Americas: A Quarterly Review of Latin American History, pp. 1-31 · publicado 2026-10-22

This article examines the history of the Taller de Escritores [Writers’ Workshop] of the University of Concepción, which existed from 1960-1963, against the backdrop of the Cold War, the Cuban Revolution, and the “boom” in Latin American literature. Although the workshop had a modest subvention from the Rockefeller Foundation, the article argues that we should understand it as the creation of a confluence of interests, and a terrain of potential contestation for Cold War politics, rather than a simple instrument of cultural diplomacy. The article describes the creation of the Taller as the product of the Encuentros de Escritores at Concepción, and the enthusiasm of the Chilean writer Fernando Alegría, then teaching at Berkeley. Although Writers’ Workshops have been described as deradicalizing forces in the U.S. context, and although a similar project (the Centro Mexicano de Escritores) received support from both the Rockefeller Foundation and the CIA in this period, there is no evidence of intelligence involvement here. Instead, Rockefeller understood the Taller as part of a package of university development. The writers in charge were left-wing and wanted to advance professional goals and respect writing as labor. Even after the Taller closed, the workshop form spread in Chile, including via participants with left-wing and anti-imperialist perspectives, suggesting that the form itself is not inherently deradicalizing, and that it depends on social context and the lived experiences of writers.

item.title: [LARR] Mexico’s Unauthorized Exits: National Ideology and The Politization of Migration in Mid-Twentieth-Century Jalisco
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Cruz de Echeverria Loebell
item.description:
Stephanie Cruz de Echeverria Loebell

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-17 · publicado 2026-10-22

In the mid-twentieth century, terms such as avalanche, grave problem, and invasion were being used on both sides of the Mexico-US border to describe the labor-related migration of Mexicans. In postrevolutionary Mexico, intellectuals, artists, and politicians were discussing which path the nation should take and what it meant to be Mexican, and the growing flow of Mexican migrants seeking temporary agricultural jobs in the United States presented a political and ideological “problem.” This article examines the conservative discourses on this issue in Jalisco’s newspaper El Informador, with a special focus on the “exclusive contributions” of two ultraconservative, Catholic intellectuals: Jesús Guisa y Azevedo and Nemesio García Naranjo. In the context of postrevolutionary nation building in Mexico, conservative critiques and the vilification of migration to the United States were attempts to attack the revolutionary project that was trying to dismantle the power structures that had prevailed since Porfirian times, threatening conservatives’ privilege and, as a result, politicizing migration. This approach shows migration not merely as an economic adaptive strategy but also a political issue that continues to be deployed in discourses surrounding national integrity of both countries.

item.title: [LARR] La historia como palimpsesto: Mendigos y criminales en la narrativa de Francisco Calcagno
item.dc:creator: María Alejandra Aguilar Dornelles
item.description:
María Alejandra Aguilar Dornelles

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-16 · publicado 2026-10-22

Este artículo examina la obra narrativa del escritor cubano Francisco Calcagno (1827–1903) y destaca su distanciamiento ideológico respecto de la novela antiesclavista cubana. A partir del análisis de su primera novela, Los crímenes de Concha, y de la última publicada, Aponte, sin perder de vista los personajes esclavizados presentes en el resto de su producción narrativa, es posible identificar la persistente recurrencia de las figuras del mendigo y del criminal. En una narrativa que se propone como histórica, Calcagno construye visiones simplificadas, dotadas de un notable poder de persuasión, que ocultan, tras un palimpsesto de imágenes nefastas, el surgimiento de la prensa negra y el protagonismo de líderes afrodescendientes. La reiterada configuración de estas figuras busca controlar la movilidad histórica y mantener a los hombres y mujeres de ascendencia africana detenidos entre el servilismo y el cimarronaje.

item.title: [LARR] Fontes para uma terceira margem: Luiza do Valle e a multiplicidade do ser indígena na Ditadura Militar
item.dc:creator: Carlos Benítez Trinidad, Hygor Mesquita Faria
item.description:
Carlos Benítez Trinidad, Hygor Mesquita Faria

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-16 · publicado 2026-10-22

Este artigo analisa a carta enviada em 1975 por Luiza do Valle, indígena Tupi e funcionária da FUNAI, ao Comando da 4ª Brigada de Infantaria, arquivada pela Assessoria de Segurança e Informações da FUNAI (ASI-FUNAI). A partir desse documento e de fontes complementares do Arquivo Nacional, do Museu do Índio e do Armazém Memória, reconstrói-se a trajetória de uma família indígena que atuou durante décadas dentro do aparato indigenista estatal, entre o Serviço de Proteção aos Índios e a Fundação Nacional do Índio. Mobilizando o conceito de “terceira margem”, inspirado em Guimarães Rosa, o estudo questiona as interpretações dicotômicas (resistência/colaboração) que dominam a historiografia sobre a história indígena na Ditadura Militar brasileira (1964–1985). A análise revela a dependência estrutural do indigenismo em relação a agentes indígenas, a continuidade da violência fundiária sobre populações racializadas e as formas de agência exercidas por uma mulher indígena dentro do sistema que a subordinava.

item.title: [LARR] Collective Action, Sex-Gender Dissidence, and Migration in Chile: Politicized Affectivities and Identities
item.dc:creator: María Fernanda Stang, Antonia Lara, Caterine Galaz Valderrama
item.description:
María Fernanda Stang, Antonia Lara, Caterine Galaz Valderrama

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-19 · publicado 2026-10-22

This article analyzes how sex-gender-dissident migrants living in Chile interpret their involvement in activism. We develop an analysis based on ten in-depth interviews with LGBTI+ migrants residing in five regions of the country. We identify two interpretative repertoires regarding the involvement of these individuals in activism. The first, which we call political-affective, centers on the metaphor of family to describe the organizations where our interviewees participate: these spaces offer containment and protection against the injustices they face due to their gender identity, as well as mutual help and solidarity in the face of loneliness and lack of networks. The second repertoire, which we call political identity, is based on the strategic use of an identity linked to sex-gender dissidence to advance political claims. This use challenges the heteropatriarchal order and also, based on these migrants’ foreignness, the national framework upon which the nation-state is constructed.

item.dc:creator: Valeria Manzano
item.description:
Valeria Manzano

Secuencia, núm. 126 · publicado 2026-10-19

Este artículo reconstruye el proceso de institucionalización del movimiento de la Nueva Canción en la década de 1980, que incluyó la organización de tres festivales anuales entre 1982, 1983 y 1984 (en México, Managua y Quito, respectivamente). Este artículo busca contribuir tanto a la historia de ese movimiento como a la de la cultura política de izquierdas en América Latina en la década de 1980. En este sentido, el artículo da cuenta de la vitalidad de esa heterogénea cultura política en la que la revolución, como proyecto e imaginario, aún tenía una gravitación fundamental. La “causa sandinista” fue el cemento que le dio cierta unidad y permitió canalizar algunas transformaciones importantes. Desde la reconstrucción morfológica de los festivales y de las comunidades creadas en torno a ellos, el artículo muestra que, gradualmente, los motivos relacionados con la “paz” ganaron preeminencia frente a motivos más sedimentados, asociados, por ejemplo, a las épicas guerrilleras.

item.title: [JLAS] Anti-Bolshevism in the Andes: José Carlos Mariátegui’s Political Thought in Context, 1917–30
item.dc:creator: Peter David Morgan
item.description:

Journal of Latin American Studies, pp. 1-27 · publicado 2026-10-19

This paper situates José Carlos Mariátegui’s Marxism in the context of emergent anti-Bolshevism in interwar Perú and Latin America. In doing so, the paper locates a moment of overlooked coherence between Mariátegui’s vernacular and universalist interpretations of Marxism during the 1920s in the pragmatic dimension of political meaning. Both Mariátegui’s conceptually national and global uses of Marxism were, in part, responding to the same, hostile context of anti-Bolshevik Othering in Perú, and they were both intended to undermine that project in order to effect the globalisation of Marxism from Europe to Latin America. The paper therefore bridges the gap between the Latin Americanist reading of Mariátegui’s thought and the more recent, global turn in scholarship, by suggesting a way to understand the different scales of Mariátegui’s Marxism holistically.

Journal of Latin American Studies, pp. 1-25 · publicado 2026-10-16

This paper tells the story of Felipe Pescador, a neighbourhood born of an occupation of railway lands by railway employees in Mexico City’s industrial corridor. Across disciplines, a rich literature on Latin America has critically examined housing struggles among marginalised and working-class people. But attention to individual, self-built settlements has remained a less common approach to the issue. Focused study provides an opportunity to critically examine how changes in the city’s political economy gradually shifted strategies to obtain shelter. As the heft of organised labour waned and the institutionalisation of housing demands increased, residents ultimately legitimated a pragmatic political practice – sometimes at odds with the policies of the official party, the PRI – and put property rights at the centre of their struggle. Historicising ties between property, law and politics thus complicates visions of informal housing struggles as necessarily progressive initiatives, as well as accounts of informal settlements as places of grassroots entrepreneurship.

El artículo examina la transformación demográfica de las Islas Malvinas tras la ocupación británica de 1833 y analiza cómo el Reino Unido implementó estrategias de colonización destinadas a consolidar y legitimar su dominio. A partir de los censos oficiales británicos entre 1833 y 1851, se evidencia el desplazamiento y la invisibilización de la población argentina, así como su reclasificación en categorías ambiguas, lo que configura un proceso sistemático de reemplazo poblacional, el cual no se limitó al plano demográfico, sino que también operó en los planos simbólico y discursivo, mediante el uso del censo como instrumento de gubernamentalidad y de legitimación ideológica. Desde un enfoque histórico-crítico, el estudio demuestra que la actual configuración poblacional del archipiélago no es fruto de una evolución natural, sino de una política imperial orientada a la ocupación, la implantación y la consolidación de una narrativa hegemónica al servicio del proyecto colonial británico.

This microhistory examines European industrial capitalism in the postcolonial Andes, focusing on the abandoned site of Changamoqo in Bolivia’s Sajama province. This place features ruins from a nineteenth-century marketplace and foundry at the base of a sacred mountain. Archaeological research, archival analysis and oral histories reveal why foreigners invested heavily in this remote Indigenous region. The site exemplifies a capitalist model developed by European immigrants and local partners, adapting the Andean premodern institution of the ‘ tambo ’. Changamoqo offers crucial insights from a bottom-up, multidisciplinary and situated perspective into the long history of postcolonial extractivism in the Andes.

item.title: [LARR] Terminator Versus Avatar in Contemporary Latin American Science Fiction
item.dc:creator: Matías Larramendi-Salvat
item.description:
Matías Larramendi-Salvat

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-16 · publicado 2026-10-12

This article examines two tendencies in contemporary Latin American science fiction, drawing on Mark Fisher’s terms Terminator and Avatar. Derived from the eponymous movies, Terminator narratives depict capitalist destruction as inevitable, while Avatar narratives imagine that global collapse can be averted by returning to premodern forms of social organization. Following Fredric Jameson, I interpret both as symbolic acts addressing climate change and the planetary devastation produced by the capitalist management of modernity. Despite their apparent opposition, both assume that modernity and technological development serve only the interests of the current social formation, with its drive for infinite economic expansion and disregard for the planet’s finite resources. Informed by the works of Agustina Bazterrica, Michel Nieva, Erick J. Mota, and Jorge Baradit, I outline a third position, alternative modernity, as theorized by Bolívar Echeverría and akin to Fisher’s postcapitalism, which reimagines technology while preserving modernity’s emancipatory potential—meeting human needs without an antagonistic stance toward nature.

This article aims to analyze the struggle led by the indigenous women of Chiapas in the defense of their rights within the framework of the Zapatista movement. I focus on how, from the visibility of the injustices that Indigenous peoples experienced, women managed to position their voice first within the movement and then outside of it, giving an account of the multiple violences they face. This analysis is based on my experience with the Chiapas Women’s Rights Center, focusing on its School of Human Rights Defenders and Promoters. From this experience I reflect on the contributions of the Zapatista national liberation movement to its thirty years of existence and how women have managed to position their voices and work to access their individual and collective rights.

item.title: [LARR] Molding the Spirit in the Twentieth Century: Converging Rodó, Vasconcelos, and Zapotec Cosmology for Zapotec Cultural Preservation and Revitalization
item.dc:creator: Angelica Waner
item.description:
Angelica Waner

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-16 · publicado 2026-10-10

In the heart of postrevolutionary Mexico, a group of Zapotec student-authors united to publish a newspaper, Neza (“road” or “path”). They wrote and published two manifestos in which they declared their goal: the preservation of the Zapotec spirit. They were inspired by the intellectual and cultural movements of the time, the Vanguardia, Rodó, and Vasconcelos, and merged those with Zapotec cosmology to call for their own continuance and that of their culture. While Zapotec literature of the Isthmus has primarily been read as a literature of nostalgia or considered folklore, this article highlights the way that the Zapotec intellectuals were in conversation with larger Latin American movements of their time and how they merge with Zapotec philosophy. This article argues that early twentieth-century Zapotec intellectuals utilized both Western and Zapotec traditions to (re)think concepts such as the spirit, thus contributing to Zapotec philosophy and ultimately enacting Zapotec futurities.

The narrative of women's emancipation is dominated by the Western European perspective. But what was the situation in the Czech lands, a culturally heterogeneous region where German, Czech and Jewish literature existed side by side? This study explores the complex processes that shaped the emergence and reception of women's literature in the Czech lands in the 1830s and 1840s. The recognition of women writers here emerges from multifaceted negotiations involving male critics, editors and gatekeepers of literature, rather than women themselves. Critics set the boundaries of acceptable women's writing: they preferred certain genres and rejected politically charged feminist voices.

item.title: [GLQ] The Queer Losses of Latinx Orpheus
item.dc:creator: Christofer A. Rodelo
item.description:

This essay reexamines the New York City Ballet's 1948 production of Orpheus, centering two of its major dancers: Nicholas Magallanes and Francisco Moncion. These two queer Latinx figures (from Mexico and the Dominican Republic, respectively) performed in the roles of Orpheus and the Dark Angel, captivating audiences and critics alike with their intimate choreography. The essay indexes this performance as an early example of how queer Latinx performance and aesthetic practices were imagined through classical Greek narratives. It argues that the tale of Orpheus, as one based in moments of loss and failure through a queer protagonist, has manifested as an apt allegory through which minoritarian subjects in the modern era can imagine their own experiences in a world where perfect outcomes are not promised. It also emphasizes the duet as a method for engaging with historical formations of queer of color aesthetics. In focusing on this rendition of Orpheus, this essay underscores its impact as part of a longer genealogy of queer Latinx philhellenism that has continued to shape Latinx expressive cultures to this day.

item.title: [GLQ] Muñoz and the Mystical Tradition
item.dc:creator: Kris Trujillo
item.description:

GLQ, vol. 32, núm. 4, pp. 483-518 · publicado 2026-10-01

José Esteban Muñoz's Cruising Utopia has assumed an emblematic status in queer of color critique's temporal orientation by cementing its attachment to the future. This association between queer of color critique and queer futurity emerges in large part from its opposition to the so-called antisocial thesis in queer theory—an opposition that is infamously staged as a conflict between Muñoz's utopianism and Lee Edelman's polemic against reproductive futurity. This essay proffers an opportunity to escape from the quagmire of this binary with a turn to the premodern past. I suggest that Muñoz's turn to religion makes available an alternative way of conceiving relationality and antirelatonality in the example of Teresa of Ávila. Ultimately, the Christian mystical tradition not only shifts queer of color critique's temporal orientation to the Middle Ages but also highlights the inseparability of queer community formation and queer negation.

This article argues that the narrator's dramatic descent into an increasingly ambivalent performance of poetic declamations of a recovered Blackness itself dramatizes a recurring rending of temporality. Instructed by Fanon's own critique of temporality as assumed by phenomenology, this article draws out the implications of such an argument for affirmations of nonlinear temporalities in literarily minded queer theory. Ultimately, in conversation with the special issue's contributions, this article reckons with the dramatized katabasis of Fanon's narrator as an ever (un)timely lesson about the racializing interdictions at work in the queer reach for a transtemporal touch of affirmation.

item.title: [GLQ] Reimagining Gender
item.dc:creator: C. Libby
item.description:
C. Libby

GLQ, vol. 32, núm. 4, pp. 535-554 · publicado 2026-10-01

Genealogies of gender's emergence as a modern analytic category typically proceed with an account of John Money and Robert Stoller's mid-twentieth-century research with intersex patients and an acknowledgment of the category's ongoing entanglement with racist, colonial, and eugenic logics. The loathsome historical connections between gender categories and sexology have prompted scholars to argue that these terms need to be rethought, unmotivated, or even relinquished. However, rather than abandoning these tools of categorization, popular queer and trans culture has recently been depicted as undergoing a “taxonomical renaissance.” This article makes sense of this discrepancy by foregrounding the ongoing influence of the medieval recombinative imagination and esoteric spiritual practices in queer and trans world making. It concludes that interpreting the current proliferation of identity categories through the lens of taxonomy risks misrecognizing the polymorphous underpinnings of queer and trans cultural production.

item.title: [GLQ] Remembering Confucian Homoeroticism
item.dc:creator: Peng Yin
item.description:
Peng Yin

GLQ, vol. 32, núm. 4, pp. 581-603 · publicado 2026-10-01

This essay probes the modes of remembering Confucian homoeroticism to unsettle Orientalist idealization and homonationalist hierarchy in anglophone scholarship. The author retrieves queer terms such as cut sleeve, male favorites, shared peach, paired eating, Longyang, a different fragrance, wildflowers, and southern wind to show how canonical disapproval of homoeroticism was imbricated with social dynamics to unpredictable effect, thus leaving enormous latitude for forging queer subjectivity. In conversation with the materialist turn in queer theory, the author argues that if our search for a queer Confucian past is limited to finding analogs to European “homosexuality” as a category of sexual identity—and if our criterion for this search is the permission/prohibition divide or the quantity of representation—we risk missing much of queer existence under Confucianism in all its textured complexity. Finally, the author asks how alternate forms of naming might indicate possibilities for queer life less bound by the preoccupations of European juridical (genital configuration), magisterial theological (gender complementarity), and psychological (sexual aim or object) modes of knowing, as well as their descendants in gay liberationist and multiculturalist discourse.

item.title: [Gender & History] Gender and Obstetric Violence in Britain, ca. 1750–1830
item.dc:creator: Paige Donaghy
item.description:
Paige Donaghy

Gender & History · publicado 2026-10-07

Obstetric violence is a form of gendered violence experienced by pregnant and birthing people, particularly women, during medical care provided in the hospital, clinic or home. Recent scholarship has explored how obstetric violence and obstetric racism manifested historically, from post‐war Canada to colonial and postcolonial Mexico. Drawing on existing work and historical studies of domestic and sexual violence, this article argues that historians can take up the framework of ‘obstetric violence’ to study past iterations of this form of gender violence. To explore these suggestions, the article traces concerns and discussions about harmful and violent midwifery and obstetric care in Britain from the mid‐eighteenth to early‐nineteenth centuries. It draws on the under‐explored records of the Royal Maternity Charity, a philanthropic organisation that provided free midwifery care to poor Londoners, and the work of obstetrician James Blundell, a midwifery lecturer at Guy's Hospital London who is credited with first using the term ‘obstetrical’ and ‘obstetric’ violence in the 1820s. Analysing these materials, the article contends that the framework of ‘obstetric violence’, understood today, helps historians map out harm done towards pregnant and birthing women in the past, in similar ways to historical configurations of familial and sexual violence.

item.title: [RIEG] El difícil camino de la institucionalización del cuidado comunitario: 40 años de lucha de las madres comunitarias en Colombia
item.dc:creator: Anayatzin Ramirez, Javier A. Pineda D.
item.description:
Anayatzin Ramirez, Javier A. Pineda D.

Revista Interdisciplinaria de Estudios de Género de El Colegio de México, vol. 12, pp. 1-40 · publicado 2026-10-05

La literatura feminista emergente sobre los cuidados ha impactado el movimiento social y las políticas públicas en Latinoamérica. No obstante, poco se sabe de los cuidados comunitarios y las experiencias en su institucionalización desde el Estado. El presente artículo analiza la trayectoria del Programa de Hogares Comunitarios de Bienestar Familiar (HCB) en Colombia, desde su creación en 1986 hasta 2025, como la principal política pública para el cuidado de la infancia, desde los aportes del institucionalismo feminista. Identifica las tensiones generadas entre el Estado y las organizaciones comunitarias en la provisión del cuidado y el papel trascendental de la agencia colectiva de las Madres Comunitarias (MC), como actoras centrales del cuidado. A partir de una metodología cualitativa, con base en testimonios de MC, se descubre que el programa de HCB se consolidó y expandió en el cuidado infantil, a costa de no reconocer el cuidado de las MC como trabajo pleno. En una trayectoria de 40 años de lucha (acciones legales, paros, etcétera), las organizaciones de MC reivindicaron el cuidado como trabajo, históricamente concebido como “vocación” femenina, en una resistencia por los derechos laborales de las cuidadoras.

item.title: [JLAS] Maduro’s Long-Lasting Strength from Weakness: How Venezuela’s Dictatorship Turned Adversity into Opportunity
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Di Bonaventura-Altuve, Kurt Weyland
item.description:
Leonardo Di Bonaventura-Altuve, Kurt Weyland

Journal of Latin American Studies, pp. 1-18 · publicado 2026-10-05

How did Nicolás Maduro’s autocratic regime in Venezuela survive serious problems and massive failures for 13 years? Contrary to the prevailing emphasis on the autocracy’s fragility, we explore the domestic and international foundations of its noteworthy resilience. Integrating Albert Hirschman’s framework of ‘Exit, Voice and Loyalty’ with Milan Svolik’s systematic theory of authoritarian rule, we highlight how exit via mass emigration, popular loyalty forged through conditional food aid, and elite loyalty engineered through corruption and patronage and reinforced by fears of international prosecution safeguarded Maduro’s dictatorship against domestic challenges that have toppled other autocracies worldwide. Only a US commando operation managed to oust the autocrat – yet nevertheless, the main structures of the non-democratic regime still seem to persist.

item.title: [LARR] La obra me curó: A Case Study of Las Curanderas Teatro and Their Theater Healing Praxis in Guatemala
item.dc:creator: Nathalia P. Hernández Ochoa
item.description:
Nathalia P. Hernández Ochoa

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-20 · publicado 2026-10-02

This article examines how Maya Kaqchikel women from Iximulew (Guatemala) conceptualize and respond to gender-based violence through a theater-making praxis rooted in ancestral healing traditions. Focusing on Las Curanderas Teatro as a case study, I theorize performing healing as an embodied practice that integrates theater making with ancestral medicinal knowledge to confront patriarchal violence shaped by the coloniality of gender and the pedagogies of cruelty. I trace this praxis in two interconnected ways: first, through performance, where curanderas and limpias are invoked to address individual and collective wounds; and second, through a theater-making methodology grounded in Indigenous healing systems. This methodology unfolds in three cyclical stages: identification of the wound(s), release and transformation, and restoration of life. Drawing on seven semistructured interviews with Las Curanderas Teatro members and multisited feminist ethnographic research (2019–2020), I argue that performing healing constitutes Indigenous women’s resurgence of cultural memory and spiritual activism—both deeply political. Through embodied ancestral knowledge and collective care, Las Curanderas Teatro advances decolonial feminist interventions that insist on healing a deeply wounded social body produced by intersecting forms of gender-based violence.

item.title: [HAHR] The Resilience of Peruvian Viceregal Patronage: Governance, Corregimientos, and Corruption Under Melchor de Navarra, 1681–1689
item.dc:creator: Rubén Gálvez Martín
item.description:
Rubén Gálvez Martín

Hispanic American Historical Review · publicado 2026-10-01

Drawing on the case of Melchor de Navarra, viceroy of Peru from 1681 to 1689, this article qualifies the thesis that viceregal patronage in the Spanish monarchy declined in the late seventeenth century. The instruments that Navarra employed for political management—particularly the provision of corregimientos—reveal that, under his rule, patronage did not recede: It became almost hegemonic and served as a channel of illicit gain for him and his circles. This conclusion rests on a relational approach and on the cross-reading of administrative and notarial sources in Spain and Peru, which make it possible to reconstruct this sphere of business with a breadth and contextual depth not previously achieved. The study sheds light on the exercise, negotiation, and legitimation of power, and on the blurred boundaries between public service and private gain in the early modern Hispanic world.
