item.title: [HAHR] The Last Asiento, “Refuse Slaves,” and “Esclavos de Desecho”: British Traffic of Captives in Trinidad, Venezuela, and Cuba in the 1780s
item.dc:creator: Alex Borucki, José Luis Belmonte Postigo
item.description:
Alex Borucki, José Luis Belmonte Postigo

Hispanic American Historical Review · publicado 2026-10-01

This article examines the negotiations between the Irish-born, Jamaica-based merchant Edward Barry and Spanish authorities beginning in 1783 to obtain and implement a slave trade contract, which then shaped the shipment of captives to colonial Venezuela and Cuba until the Spanish crown deregulated the slave trade in 1789. Although brief, this was the only time that a merchant based in the Americas, rather than in Europe, obtained the asiento, highlighting the importance of intercolonial slavers. Because the categorization of captives as “refuse slaves” became contentious, we analyze Barry's case to explore how this term was defined in Spanish through the stories of these enslaved Africans. Extracting value from the broken bodies of the sick, the disabled, and the dying was a core activity of slave traders, especially for those, like Barry, based in the Americas, with dreadful implications for the trafficked Africans, particularly the women and children.

item.title: [HAHR] “The Prelude to Our Dissolution”: Paper Money and National Sovereignty in Mexico's First Empire
item.dc:creator: Andrew Konove
item.description:
Andrew Konove

Hispanic American Historical Review · publicado 2026-10-01

This article examines Mexico's short-lived first experiment with paper money in the years immediately following the country's independence from Spain. Challenging the traditional explanation for the money's failure, which attributed it to the Mexican public's long-standing attachment to silver coins, it argues that the project ran aground because of its competing financial, political, and social objectives and the resistance that it encountered from the commercial sector. Using sources from Mexico's national archives, published proceedings of its constituent congress, newspapers, and pamphlet literature from the era, the study reveals a previously unrecognized nation-building agenda that sought to turn Mexico's citizens into lenders and to subordinate Spanish merchant capitalists to the fledgling state. It contributes to the history of early national Mexico and, comparing the project to other contemporaneous paper money experiments, to the interconnected histories of money and state formation.

item.title: [HAHR] Sodomy, Slavery, and Childhood in Early Colonial San Luis Potosí: A 1602 Criminal Case
item.dc:creator: José Armando Hernández Soubervielle
item.description:
José Armando Hernández Soubervielle

Hispanic American Historical Review · publicado 2026-10-01

This article examines a 1602 criminal case prosecuted in the frontier town of San Luis Potosí, in which Sebastián, a free Indigenous adult, and Diego, an enslaved Black child between six and eight years old, were both tried for sodomy. Drawing on the criminal proceedings preserved in the Archivo Histórico del Estado de San Luis Potosí, the analysis explores how colonial hierarchies of age, legal status, calidad, and gender intersected to create extreme vulnerability and shape juridical outcomes. The case reveals the slaveholding colonial legal system's “fantasy of consent”: its apparent disinterest in distinguishing coercion from consent when prosecuting sodomy involving minors. By recovering Diego's mediated yet irreplaceable voice from the archive, this study contributes to the historiography of African-Indigenous relations, enslaved childhood, and the regulation of sexuality in early colonial New Spain.

item.title: [Historia y Grafía] La administración de tres haciendas durante la Revolución
item.dc:creator: María Eugenia Ponce Alcocer
item.description:
María Eugenia Ponce Alcocer

Historia y Grafía, núm. 34, pp. 76-107 · publicado 2026-03-11

The article analyzes how the Mexican Revolution affected life in three haciendas in the central region of Mexico-Tlaxcala and the State of Mexico; and how this businesses managed to face the difficulties and continue both production and commercialization of their products. Marauding, requisition of goods and outright military occupation of the haciendas –on the part of revolutionary forces– are some of the problems which were experimented during the years of 1911 still 1918; but also new taxes and forced loans implemented by diverse state and federal authorities in order to sustain their hegemony. item.title: [Historia y Grafía] ¿Debemos seguir escribiendo historias de la literatura?
item.dc:creator: Hans Ulrich Gumbrecht
item.description:
Hans Ulrich Gumbrecht

Historia y Grafía, núm. 34, pp. 111-132 · publicado 2026-03-11

The title-question is serious, i.e. it is not geared to produce a self-congratu- latory answer for the tradition of literary studies and its historical work. But the reason that makes this question serious has little (if anything) to do with interior movements in the discipline of “Literary Studies.” Rather, this essay departs from the thesis that, over the past three or four decades, the “chronotype” (the construction of time) in which we (the “western” cultures, and perhaps even “global culture”) are living, has undergone a profound transformation; and that this transformation makes obsolete the central as- sumption that had founded not only “Literary History,” as a genre, for more than two centuries -- i.e. the assumption that one could “learn” (learn how to make prognostics) from the historical unfolding of any phenomenon, with “literature” being an eminent case in point. If this “historicist” chronotope is no longer ours, then the question arises of what among our new relationship to the textual body called “literature” may qualify as specifically “historical,” and which types of new discourses they might enhance.

item.title: [Historia y Grafía] Representación historiográfica: relato e intencionalidad.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Flores
item.description:
Roberto Flores

Historia y Grafía, núm. 34, pp. 133-163 · publicado 2026-03-11

If indisputably historiography refers to the past, the manner in which it does is subject to debate. Historical events are directly inexpressible and tend to become a narrative of occurrences: by doing so they jeopardize the proper sequentiality of accounts. The objective of this paper is to question sequentiality under the light of the phenomenological theories of intentionality, in particular that of the double orientation of time, retentive and protentive. From this perspective, historiographical representation is conceived as the process of recreating an event, a recreation on the part of the reader of the history of another’s experience, and not as a reference to historical events. An analysis of a fragment from fray Bernardino de Sahagun’s Florentine Codex (xvi century) will illustrate this argument and expose the way in which the narrative itself appeals to the interpretative collaboration of the history’s receiver.

item.title: [Historia y Grafía] Las imágenes de viajeros en el siglo XIX. El caso de los grabados de Charles Saffray sobre Colombia
item.dc:creator: Santiago Muñoz Arbelaez
item.description:
Santiago Muñoz Arbelaez

Historia y Grafía, núm. 34, pp. 165-197 · publicado 2026-03-11

In 1861, Charles Saffray travelled through New Granada drawing and writing about what he saw. Ten years after his voyage, his narrative was published in the important journal Le Tour du Monde, accompanied by en- gravings that were meant to help readers visualize the narrative. By analyz- ing three engravings, this article analyzes the ‘way of seeing’ behind Saffray’s texts and images. The article shows that, instead of being neutral, the im- ages presented a ‘way of seeing’ the environment according to the interest of Nineteenth-Century European expansionists. item.title: [The Americas] “ In the Footsteps of Our Elders ”: Franciscan Missionary Lore and Collective Identity and Memory in Colonial and Nineteenth-Century Mexico

item.description:

The essay explores Franciscan missionary lore in colonial and nineteenth-century Mexico, focusing on the interplay between ordinary and extraordinary events as narrated by missionaries. It challenges traditional views that prioritize chronicles and hagiographies by underscoring the significance of more succinct, episodic writings which also played a role in fostering communal identity and institutional memory. These shorter narratives, while inward-facing and didactic, reveal how Franciscans navigated the boundary between the anticipated and the unexpected, transforming everyday occurrences and remarkable incidents into a tapestry of missionary lore that reinforced both solidarity among friars and the legitimacy of their evangelical mission. By aligning with broader historiographical perspectives emphasizing the role of narrative in shaping religious identity and institutional memory, the essay contributes to understanding how Franciscans actively crafted a narrative universe in which the miraculous, the pedagogical, and the communal intertwined. The essay demonstrates how the construction of Franciscan missionary lore was not just about recounting remarkable miracles or heroic sacrifices but about cultivating a sense of belonging and continuity through the ritualized retelling of everyday and exceptional events. This approach invites further scholarly engagement with Franciscan texts and encourages a reevaluation of how religious communities negotiated memory, identity, and authority through storytelling.

item.title: [The Americas] Dancing to Foreign Rhythms, Making Them Our Own: The Nicaraguan Foxtrot on the Global Stage, 1919–1933

item.description:

Music accompanied the US intervention in Nicaragua. Above all other genres, US popular music dominated Nicaraguan culture beginning in 1919. And it never left. This article examines the foxtrot, a wildly popular US music and social dance, as a lens for understanding how Nicaraguans saw themselves, how they negotiated the intervention, and how they acted upon the world. It argues that Nicaraguans developed new musical expressions, making foreign culture their own, despite the dominance of US intervention. Through transculturation, Nicaraguans maintained a sense of national identity. More than an entertainment, the foxtrot grew into a discourse for reckoning with US intervention and contesting Nicaraguan cultural values. Remarkably, the transnational circulation of the Nicaraguan foxtrot resonated beyond Central America, putting Nicaraguan music on the global stage. The first section traces the origins and transmission of the foxtrot during the ragtime era between the 1890s and 1917, followed by the early jazz period. The second section narrates the foxtrot’s 1919 arrival and rooting as a popular music in western Nicaragua. The third section surveys the foxtrot’s domestic and transnational dissemination via Nicaraguan entertainments and US recording companies from 1919 to 1933. The fourth section explores the cultural embrace of the foxtrot in Nicaragua during that same period. Conversely, the fifth section pursues its literary critiques. The sixth and final section examines Nicaraguan composer Luis A. Delgadillo as a prominent advocate and critic of the foxtrot. The conclusion places the Nicaraguan foxtrot in context of greater Latin American production.

We analyze the social protection policy response to COVID-19 and its impact on household incomes in Uruguay during 2020 and 2021, using static microsimulation methods. From the onset of the crisis, the Uruguayan government implemented adjustments to existing social protection policies as well as a new transfer and an emergency tax. Our results indicate that Uruguay’s enhanced social protection system prevented poverty from increasing by 2.8 and 3.7 percentage points in 2020 and 2021, respectively. The COVID-19 enhancements contributed 1.3 and 1.6 percentage points of this total protective effect. The effects were bigger among households with children. The most important instruments were unemployment insurance in 2020 and the conditional cash transfer directed at households with children in 2021. Taken together, these modifications to the social protection system prevented the Gini index from increasing by around 0.7 additional percentage points.

This article examines how algorithmic mediation reshapes religious leadership and trust in contemporary China. Public scandals and satirical works reveal deepening disillusionment with monks’ wealth-seeking behaviors and moral failings. Satire and distrust expose fragile conditions under which religious trust becomes unstable and contested. The article advances digital religion research and highlights significant implications for policymakers, religious organizations, technology platforms, and scholars of culture and society.

The 1990s were a vexed time for feminists in Britain. Cultural commentators declared that feminism's key battles had been won, and that given women's ascendency across various political and cultural barometers of success, the country was entering a newly ‘postfeminist’ era. At the same time, feminist groups identified sites of resurgence and growth in the wake of the fragmentation of the movement's ‘second wave’. Towards the end of the decade, momentum gathered around the concept of a ‘New Feminism’ – one that was popular, mainstream, focused on the material rather than the personal, and that was unshackled from feminism's recent past. This feminism, advanced by prominent advocates like 30‐year‐old Natasha Walter, reflected the rhetorical and policy posture of the New Labour government. Like New Labour, the ‘new feminism’ sought to chart a centrist route through the political waters and disavowed its radical history in service of what it hailed as a defiantly pragmatic future. This article interrogates the trajectory of the ‘new feminism’ in 1990s Britain, examining its place within wider feminist conversations, political discourses and positioning it in relation to growing anxieties about masculinity, men and boys.

This article examines how Vietnamese women converted wartime military legitimacy into sustained peace‐building authority during and after the Vietnam War (1954–2007). It argues that the primary mechanism was not combat experience alone but the triple burden the Vietnamese Communist Party imposed on women – requiring simultaneous excellence in agricultural production, combat or defence service and domestic care. This asymmetric demand, with no male equivalent, inadvertently cultivated cross‐domain competencies in logistics coordination, community mobilisation and coalition‐building that proved directly transferable to post‐conflict diplomacy and governance. Drawing on feminist peace theories, archival materials and memoirs, the article identifies three enabling factors: the strategic instrumentalisation of cultural memory of female warrior figures to legitimise women's expanded wartime roles; the Ba đảm đang campaign, which institutionalised the triple burden; and the transferable skills this burden produced. These dynamics are traced through the story of Nguyễn Thị Định, whose guerrilla command led to her presidency of the Vietnam Women's Union (1982–92), andNguyễn Thị Bình, whose underground organising translated into her leadership at the Paris Peace Talks. The article concludes that the inequity of the triple burden paradoxically produced post‐war advantage, offering a distinctive model of female agency with broader implications for inclusive peacebuilding.

item.title: [RIEG] Que la niña mayor ayude: Hijas e hijos primogénitos en el hogar y el trabajo doméstico no remunerado
item.dc:creator: Adriana Robles
item.description:
Adriana Robles

Revista Interdisciplinaria de Estudios de Género de El Colegio de México, vol. 12, pp. 1-25 · publicado 2026-09-14

La asignación de trabajo doméstico no remunerado puede constituirse como un mecanismo mediante el cual niños, niñas y adolescentes adoptan responsabilidades y expectativas diferenciadas según su género. En este contexto, el involucramiento en estas actividades permite observar procesos de transmisión intergeneracional de normas y roles de género. El objetivo de este estudio cuantitativo es describir el tiempo destinado al trabajo doméstico no remunerado de niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA) primogénitos y evaluar cómo el sexo se asocia con dicha asignación en los países de Chile, Costa Rica, Ecuador y Paraguay, por medio de encuestas de uso del tiempo. El análisis de los primogénitos resulta relevante debido a que suelen ocupar posiciones de mayor responsabilidad en el hogar y pueden desempeñar un papel central en la organización doméstica. Los resultados muestran que las niñas y adolescentes primogénitas destinan significativamente más tiempo al trabajo doméstico no remunerado que sus pares hombres en los cuatro países analizados. Asimismo, esta desigualdad no es exclusiva de los primogénitos, ya que también se observan mayores cargas de trabajo doméstico entre las hijas menores. En conjunto, los hallazgos evidencian que la configuración por edad y sexo de los NNA dentro del hogar se asocia con divisiones desiguales del trabajo doméstico y con la reproducción de roles de género.

item.title: [LARR] Todos Contamos: Mapping the Statistical Visibility of the African Diaspora in Twenty-First-Century Latin America
item.dc:creator: Marcelo Paixão, Ricardo Henrique Lowe
item.description:
Marcelo Paixão, Ricardo Henrique Lowe

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-28 · publicado 2026-09-14

This article provides a comparative analysis of the taxonomies and categorical frameworks used to identify Afro-descendant populations in Latin America across the 2010 and 2020 census rounds. These rounds mark the first time in the region’s postcolonial history that all countries included at least one ethno-racial question targeting Afro-descendants. The results suggest that most national statistical offices elicit responses from Afro-descendants through a multicultural approach to enumeration, including questions on ancestry, cultural customs, and group belonging. Conversely, many of these ethnic -based question formulations paradoxically employ racial categories to classify Afro-descendant responses, such as negro, mulato, and moreno. These findings suggest that the growing statistical visibility of Afro-descendants in the region is partly shaped by negotiations between national statistical offices and stakeholders over categories that render Afro-descendant populations identifiable to the state as distinct ethno-racial groups. These negotiations have significant implications in a region where census classifications often serve as a basis for securing identity-based collective rights and legal protections under a “new Latin American constitutionalism,” in which Afro-descendants seemingly must rearticulate their relationships with the state from “a rubric of race to one of ethnicity.”

item.title: [JLAS] Women in Conservative Religious Mobilization in Latin America: Chile and Mexico in Comparative Perspective
item.dc:creator: Isabel Castillo, Camilla Reuterswärd
item.description:
Isabel Castillo, Camilla Reuterswärd

Journal of Latin American Studies, pp. 1-27 · publicado 2026-09-14

Studies of ‘anti-gender’ mobilisations focus on contested gender policies such as abortion, same-sex marriage and sex education. Who engages in these protests and why is less known. We argue that conservative women organise to defend religious beliefs and agendas against a perceived threat that targets not only religious institutions but also their own identities as wives and mothers by offering alternatives to conventional family structures. This argument applies to the secularisation threat of the early twentieth century as well as the policy demands of liberal social movements in the early twenty-first century. Focusing on Chile and Mexico, we highlight continuity and change in conservative–religious women’s activism.

item.title: [JLAS] Business Actors, Repression and Justice: The Role of Tucumán’s Sugar Mills in Crimes against Workers
item.dc:creator: Silvia Gabriela Nassif
item.description:
Silvia Gabriela Nassif

Journal of Latin American Studies, pp. 1-25 · publicado 2026-09-14

This article examines the role of business sectors in crimes against humanity – specifically in violence perpetrated against workers – as well as progress in accountability for their participation in such crimes, with specific reference to the Tucumán sugar mills of La Fronterita and Concepción. This historical analysis explains how in Tucumán – whose central activity is still the sugar agro-industry – the corporate sector participated in the repression and subjugation of workers. It also shows that local economic actors held significant power to obstruct any resulting Memory, Truth and Justice processes. However, local social institutions, organisations and human rights actors have marshalled their resources and designed strategies to fight back, and they have sometimes achieved notable successes.

item.title: [LARR] The Remnants of Slavery: The Description of Black Corpses in Cirilo Villaverde’s Cecilia Valdés or El Angel Hill (1882)
item.dc:creator: Ingrid Brioso Rieumont
item.description:
Ingrid Brioso Rieumont

Latin American Research Review, pp. 1-20 · publicado 2026-09-14

Cecilia Valdés or El Angel Hill (1882), by Cirilo Villaverde, is often read as a Cuban antislavery novel, yet its treatment of the remains of formerly enslaved people has received little scholarly attention. This article examines the scenes following the suicides of Pedro and Pablo Carabalí, focusing on the interval between death and burial—what I term afterdeath. In these scenes, the novel stages a tension between the narrator’s foregrounding of the corpses through description and their erasure by the enslaver characters in dialogue. This tension reveals that the decomposing bodies function as “unproductive remnants” that resist the novel’s speculative logic of valuation and cannot be recuperated under contemporary insurance practices. By foregrounding decay rather than spectrality, the study delineates the limits of commodification in the nineteenth-century Atlantic world and argues that the corpses constitute a critical site for re-thinking representations of death, value, and resistance in slave societies.

item.title: [Gender & History] “Women of the Happy Life”: Prostitution, Public Morality, and Venereal Disease in US‐Occupied Nicaragua, 1912–33
item.dc:creator: Eimeel Castillo
item.description:
Eimeel Castillo

Gender & History · publicado 2026-09-10

During the years of the US occupation (1912–33), Nicaragua's government legally regulated prostitution. Convinced of their objectives to protect society's moral and public health, politicians embarked on a long struggle to apprehend, quarantine, and segregate female prostitutes nationwide. Through a comparative analysis of these codes, this article discusses the language and changes in these regulations to examine the extent to which the broader context of US intervention shaped local perceptions and actions regarding non‐elite female sexuality. Mostly ineffective in its enforcement, the control of prostitution reinforced a model of femininity based upon ideals of modesty, discretion, and sexual purity.

item.title: [Gender & History] Partitioned Desires: Female Agency and Interfaith Relationships Around the Partition of India
item.dc:creator: Angad Singh
item.description:
Angad Singh

Gender & History · publicado 2026-09-10

Through an examination of the phenomenon of abduction, I suggest that the preoccupation with women's violation during the 1947 Partition of India has obfuscated a history of female desire. Considering accusations of kidnapping made by women's families against men belonging to a different religion in instances of interfaith desire, I demonstrate that abduction operated as a category families mobilized to control female sexuality both prior to, and during, the Partition. In privileging women's agency and desire in my historical account, I challenge the feminist positing of sexual violence as the hegemonic category for the consideration of gender during the Partition.

item.title: [Religion & Gender] Rethinking the Agency of Gay Christian Men: A Scoping Review of the Social Science Research
item.dc:creator: David Eduardo Vilchis Carrillo
item.description:
David Eduardo Vilchis Carrillo

Religion and Gender, pp. 1-29 · publicado 2026-09-08

This article presents a scoping review of fifty-four social science studies on the intersection of religious and sexual identities among gay Christian men. Although research consistently portrays LGBTQ + Christians as active agents rather than passive subjects of religious doctrine, few studies explicitly engage with theories of agency. Drawing on debates in feminist scholarship on women in conservative religious contexts, this article reinterprets existing findings through four forms of agency: resistant, empowerment, instrumental, and compliant. Applying this framework broadens understandings of gay Christian agency beyond individualist and resistance-centered interpretations by highlighting how agency is negotiated within specific religious and social contexts. It further shows that compliance may involve actively reworking religion rather than merely adapting to it. Overall, the article offers a more nuanced understanding of the diverse ways gay believers negotiate religious and sexual identities and contributes to theorizing agency in the study of gay Christians.
